pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–13 years

- **Topic:** Reading Distance-Time Graphs

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Motion):** Representing journeys with distance–time graphs and interpreting the gradient of a straight segment as speed (flat = stationary, steeper = faster); part of KS3 motion and the working-scientifically expectation to present and interpret data graphically.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS SEP — Analyzing and Interpreting Data):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS3-1] identify linear relationships; describe an object's motion from a graph of position vs time (supports MS-PS2 Motion and Stability) and CCSS-Math graphing of proportional relationships.

- **Operational details:** Reading and plotting distance-time graphs is a representational skill: pupils must come to see the LINE as an abstract record of the relationship between distance and time, not a picture of the journey's terrain. The single most important instructional move is to repeatedly and explicitly couple each segment of the line to a described motion (moving away, stopped, returning, fast vs slow), ideally in real time so the pupil watches the line being generated by movement. Speed is read from the GRADIENT (steepness), not from a value on the axis: a flat line means stationary, a steeper line means faster, and lines sloping the opposite way mean travelling back towards the start. Average speed over a straight segment is found as distance ÷ time for that segment.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal/quantitative). Interpreting a distance-time graph is a formal-operational, fully quantitative skill: the line must be read as an abstract record of a distance–time relationship, with speed extracted from the gradient. The decisive threshold is overcoming the deeply persistent graph-as-picture misconception (slope = a hill) and the slope-height confusion — errors that survive to college level — so mastery means reading flat = stationary, steeper = faster, opposite slope = returning, and computing a segment's average speed as distance ÷ time for that segment.
bestPractices: Use real-time motion sensors / data-loggers so pupils see the graph draw itself as an object (or the pupil) moves — directly coupling movement to line and breaking the 'picture' reading (IOP Spark 'Speedy graphs').
Use embodied 'walk-the-graph' activities: pupils physically walk a journey along a marked line while the class predicts the shape, grounding the abstraction in lived motion.
Draw attention to the axes and units FIRST ('What does the vertical axis tell us? What does the origin represent?') before interpreting any feature.
Go through interpretation step-by-step, linking each line segment to a specific motion, and repeat this mapping many times across varied journeys (Oak National Academy).
Explicitly teach gradient = speed and contrast it with reading a single height value; use predict-observe-explain so pupils commit to a reading before checking.
Use story/journey narration ('describe what is happening at each stage — moving, stopped, returning') and the reverse task: sketch the graph from a written journey.
keyRepresentations: The distance-time graph itself (axes labelled, origin discussed)
Real-time motion-sensor / data-logger trace (movement generates the line live)
Embodied 'graph walker' — a marked distance line on the floor walked against a timer
Journey narration cards matched to graph segments (verbal description ↔ line feature)
Annotated segments: flat = stationary, steep = fast, opposite slope = returning
commonMisconceptions: Graph-as-picture (iconic confusion): reading the line as a literal picture of terrain — e.g. an upward slope means 'walking up a hill' (Clement 1985; IOP Spark; persists to college level).
Slope-height confusion: judging speed from a point's height on the axis instead of the line's gradient (McDermott et al.; ~half of science students err).
Reading a distance or time value off the graph and calling it the speed — forgetting speed needs BOTH distance and time (Oak National Academy).
Assuming the line must start at the origin (0,0) even when the object begins at a distance from the reference point.
Drawing physically impossible graphs — vertical lines (infinite speed) or lines going 'backwards' in time.
Confusing a distance-time graph with a speed-time/velocity-time graph and interpreting features accordingly.

learn.summary: Help 10–13 year-olds read distance-time graphs by treating the LINE as an abstract record of a distance–time relationship, not a picture of terrain. The decisive goal is overcoming the graph-as-picture misconception (upward slope = 'walking up a hill') and slope-height confusion (judging speed by how high the line is rather than how steep). Learners should map each line segment to a motion (moving away, stopped, returning, fast vs slow), read speed from the gradient (flat = stationary, steeper = faster; when the vertical axis shows distance from the start, a downward slope = returning), translate both directions between a written journey and a graph, and compute a segment's average speed as distance ÷ time. A live motion-and-graph coupling is the primary vehicle; card-matching, annotated reference graphs, and embodied walk-the-graph activities are complementary.

activities.title: Two-pane motion grapher: watch the line draw itself
feedback: If a learner says the rising line means 'going uphill', replay DRIVE mode on the flat track and point out the track is level while the line still rises — the rise records distance covered over time.

When a learner drags a segment steeper expecting the cart to climb, highlight that the cart only moves faster: 'the line was never a hill; it records distance over time, and its steepness shows speed.'
Point to the flat segment and name it: distance is not changing while time passes, so the object is stopped — not 'on flat ground'.
Use the live gradient readout to show that steeper = faster and that two segments at different heights with the same steepness mean the same speed.
activities.rationale: The core difficulty is connecting motion to an abstract line; generating and manipulating that coupling in real time directly confronts the graph-as-picture misconception. Research recommends real-time motion sensors and predict-observe-explore moves that couple movement to line.
sourceClaims: Pupils interpret distance-time/speed-time graphs as literal pictures (e.g. slope = going uphill); recommended responses include real-time motion sensors and BEST diagnostics.
learnerActions: In DRIVE mode, send a cart along a straight track with distance markers and a clock, and watch a distance-time graph plot live beneath it in lockstep.
Stop the cart and observe the line go flat; send the cart back toward the start and observe the line slope downward (the graph plots the cart's distance from the start).
Make the cart go fast and then slow, and compare how the line's steepness changes with a live 'speed = gradient' readout.
In BUILD mode, drag a graph segment steeper, predict what the cart will do, then watch: the cart zooms faster along the FLAT track rather than 'climbing'.
Explore a deliberately 'hill-shaped' journey scene and explain why the line is still just a record of distance over time, not a picture of a hill.
activities.intendedInsight: The line is a record of the relationship between distance and time; its steepness means speed, not terrain. Making the line steeper makes the object faster — it does not make the object climb.

activities.title: Walk the graph (embodied journey)
feedback: If a learner describes the flat section as 'flat ground', restate that standing still means distance is not changing even though time keeps passing.
When predictions differ, walk the journey again slowly and build the line segment by segment so the mapping is explicit.
activities.rationale: Embodied 'walk-the-graph' activities link physical movement to graph shape and are a recommended best practice for grounding the abstraction in real motion; this proposal is not directly tied to a specific source claim.
learnerActions: Walk a journey along a marked distance line on the floor against a timer while classmates predict the shape of the resulting graph.
Pause partway (stand still) and discuss what the line does during that pause.
Walk back toward the start and note how the graph's slope changes direction (it slopes downward because the graph shows distance from the start).
Compare a fast walk and a slow walk and connect the difference to the steepness of the segments.
activities.intendedInsight: Grounding the abstraction in lived motion builds the motion→line link: stopping produces a flat section, returning toward the start produces a downward slope (when distance is measured from the start), and faster walking produces a steeper line.

activities.title: Read the axes and narrate each stage
feedback: If a learner names the highest point as fastest, compare two segments' steepness directly: speed is steepness, not height, and the highest point may be where the object has stopped.
If a learner reads a single distance or time value and calls it the speed, point out that speed needs BOTH a change in distance and the time taken — one axis reading alone cannot give it.
Check that learners do not assume the line starts at the origin (0,0) when the object starts some way from the reference point; the line then begins partway up the distance axis.
activities.rationale: Guiding pupils step by step, attending to axes and units first, and repeatedly linking each segment to a motion addresses the common error of reading a single value as the speed and the slope-height confusion.
sourceClaims: Teachers should guide pupils step by step through interpreting d-t graphs, linking each line with a motion repeatedly; pupils can wrongly read a distance/time value as the speed; flat line = stationary, steeper gradient = faster.
The 'graph as picture' misconception (global and feature correspondence) and slope-height confusion were taxonomised by Clement; students draw a 'hill' for speed-vs-time and persist at college level.
learnerActions: Before interpreting any feature, state what the vertical axis measures, what the horizontal axis measures, and what the origin represents.
Describe, stage by stage, what is happening on a given graph — moving away, stopped, returning, fast or slow.
Identify the fastest section by finding the STEEPEST segment (greatest gradient), not the highest point.
Calculate the average speed of one straight segment as distance ÷ time for that segment, using the axis scales.
activities.intendedInsight: Speed is read from the gradient of a segment (distance ÷ time), while the horizontal flat section means stationary; the highest point is not necessarily the fastest.

activities.title: Translate both ways: match and sketch
feedback: If a learner sketches a described journey as a literal picture (a hill for speeding up), compare it to a correct concave-up curve and re-link steepness to speed.
For 'speeding up smoothly', confirm the line gets progressively steeper rather than jumping to a straight diagonal (which would be constant speed).
In a two-line comparison, confirm 'fastest' is chosen by the steeper line, not the one that reaches higher.
A vertical line (infinite speed) or a line going backwards in time is physically impossible — flag and discuss why.
activities.rationale: A canonical formative-assessment task matches verbal interpretations to graphs to surface picture-readers; the translate-from-description step is where iconic readers reproduce a literal picture, making it strongly diagnostic. This is best used as a check after the generative interactive, not as the first teacher.
sourceClaims: A formative-assessment lesson built to identify students who read distance-time graphs as pictures rather than abstract representations; uses small-group matching of verbal interpretations to graphs.
learnerActions: Match journey descriptions (e.g. 'she stopped for lunch, then hurried home') to the correct graph segments or whole graphs, in small groups.
Sketch a distance-time graph from a written journey that includes stops and speed changes, including a return to the start.
Sketch the graph for a cyclist who sets off slowly and speeds up smoothly — a curve that starts shallow and gets steeper (concave up), not a straight line and not a hill-shaped picture.
Order four runners by speed by comparing the gradients of their lines.
Point to a place on your own sketch where the object is stopped and explain how the graph shows it.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent interpretation means translating in both directions between a written journey and the graph, treating the graph as an abstract distance-time relationship rather than a literal picture of the route.

activities.title: Annotated reference graph (recap)
feedback: Reinforce that the steep label points to gradient, not to how high the line sits.
Prompt the learner to generate the label themselves before revealing it.
activities.rationale: A static tap-to-reveal reference can usefully label segments and serve as a recap, but nothing moves, so it is a scaffold rather than the means of forging the motion→line link.
learnerActions: Use a pre-drawn, annotated distance-time graph (distance measured from the start) where each segment is labelled: flat = stationary, steep = fast, downward slope = returning toward the start.
Tap or lift a flap on the flat part to confirm 'stopped', and on the steep part to confirm 'fastest — look at the gradient'.
Use it as a quick recap or reference card when interpreting new graphs.
activities.intendedInsight: A clean labelled reference consolidates the segment-to-motion vocabulary once the motion→line link has been built elsewhere.

constraints: The annotated reference graph is a recap/reference scaffold: because nothing moves, it does not by itself build the motion→line link needed to overcome the graph-as-picture misconception; use it after generative activity, not as the primary teacher.

Card-matching and multiple-choice checks assess interpretation well but do not by themselves elicit independent construction; pair them with sketch-from-description tasks that require learners to produce a graph.
Keep deliberately tempting distractors (e.g. 'fastest = highest point', 'flat = flat ground') to surface misconceptions, but always resolve them explicitly — never leave them as valid answers.
Distance-time graphing uses two scalar axes and is inherently planar; a 3D rendering adds spatial cost and may reinforce the 'graph is a scene' confusion, so it is not recommended here.
Reading a graph is a representational mapping skill with no persona dimension to exploit, so open-ended role-play dialogue is a poor fit for this particular objective.
When describing 'slowly then speeding up', the correct graph is a concave-up curve (progressively steeper), not a straight diagonal (constant speed) and not a hill-shaped picture.
Do not assume the line must start at the origin; an object may begin at a distance from the reference point.
Distinguish a distance-time graph from a speed-time/velocity-time graph; features are interpreted differently and should not be conflated.
Two segments at different heights with the same steepness represent the same speed; height alone does not indicate speed.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Three of the four sources are marked verified:false in the source row (Oak National Academy, Clement 1985, Shell Centre MAP); treat their claims as cited but not independently re-checked here. IOP Spark is the one marked verified:true.

The legacy entry frames the live-manipulation interactive as the single artefact that 'breaks' the misconception and labels static/3D/dialogue formats as unable to teach it. Softened to affordance/limit statements: a static reference can still teach vocabulary, and a card-match can be used during teaching — comparative necessity is not established by catalog fit ratings.

The embodied walk-the-graph activity is a best practice from the pedagogy notes but is not directly supported by any source[].claim, so its sourceClaims is []; the IOP Spark claim concerns sensor-based real-time coupling specifically.

Self-audit: segment-to-motion mappings (flat = stationary, steeper = faster, downward slope = returning, average speed = distance ÷ time per segment) and the concave-up sketch for 'speeding up smoothly' are internally consistent. The DRIVE/BUILD claim that a steeper line means a faster cart on a flat track (not a climb) is physically correct for a distance-time graph.

probeDeeper: Now draw the graph for a cyclist who rides fast, stops for lunch, then rides home even faster. What does 'home' look like on the graph?
Two lines on one graph — which cyclist is faster, the steeper line or the shallower one? How do you know?
The line goes up as a straight diagonal. Is the cyclist speeding up, slowing down, or going at a steady speed? How can you tell?
Point to a place on YOUR sketch where the cyclist is stopped, and explain how the graph shows it.
assess.correctAnswer: Fastest is the STEEPEST section (greatest gradient) — the first steep rise — not the highest point. The horizontal flat part means the cyclist is STOPPED (distance not changing while time passes), not 'riding on flat ground'. The 'slowly then speeding up' sketch is a curve that starts shallow and gets steeper (concave up), not a straight line and not a hill-shaped picture.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The flat bit means the cyclist is on flat, level ground.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Map each segment to a motion in real time (walk-the-graph or a motion sensor); a horizontal line = distance not changing = stopped.
errorPatterns.distractor: The flat part means the cyclist is riding along flat, level ground.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the horizontal section as terrain rather than as stopped.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The cyclist is fastest where the line is highest up the graph.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare gradients directly: speed is steepness, not height; the highest point may be where they've stopped.
errorPatterns.distractor: Fastest is where the line reaches the highest point on the graph.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Picks the top of the graph as fastest instead of the steepest gradient.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The number the line reaches IS the speed.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Speed comes from the CHANGE in distance over time (the gradient), not a single axis reading.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reads a distance value off the axis and calls it the speed.

responseLevels.gap: Reads the graph as a picture of the route (flat = flat ground, up = uphill) and/or judges speed by height; can't translate a description into a correct sketch.
responseLevels.full: Interprets gradient as speed and horizontal as stationary, compares speeds by steepness not height, and translates fluently between a written journey and a distance-time graph (including returns to the start), treating the graph as an abstract distance-time relationship.
responseLevels.partial: Reads individual features correctly (a flat line = stopped) and finds speed from one section, but can't translate BOTH ways — e.g. sketches a described journey as a literal picture, or judges 'fastest' by height in a two-line comparison.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a distance-time graph of a cyclist's trip: it rises steeply, then flattens into a horizontal line, then rises gently. Point to the part where the cyclist is going FASTEST, and tell me what the flat horizontal part means. Then sketch the graph for a cyclist who sets off slowly and speeds up smoothly.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The graph-as-picture error (Clement 1985) makes a child read the line as the route — a flat section as 'flat ground', a rising line as 'going uphill' — and slope-height confusion makes them judge speed by how HIGH the line is rather than how STEEP. A child reading it abstractly picks the steepest part as fastest, reads the horizontal as stationary, and draws increasing steepness for speeding up. The translate step (sketch from a description) is where iconic readers reproduce a literal picture.
